title: Why do we hate?
hook: Sakka, king of the gods, asks why beings who wish to live without hate still live in hate

segments.voice: Yesterday: a jeweled city returned to thatch, and your line, it was grand once, and it's gone. What fine thing did you enjoy, knowing it would pass? Today, a king of the gods arrives with a musician and a question. Day five hundred fifty-four.
screen: `IT WAS GRAND ONCE, AND IT'S GONE.`

segments.voice: Before the question, a love song. Sakka, king of the gods, wants to see the Buddha, who is sitting in a cave in the hills near Rajagaha. He doesn't just walk in. He sends ahead a celestial musician, Pancasikha, with a lute. Pancasikha stands near the cave and sings a song that mixes praise of the Buddha with longing for a girl he loves. The Buddha listens, and then tells him, kindly: the strings and your voice blend well. Then Sakka comes in, and asks his question. Today: why do we hate?
screen: `A LOVE SONG OUTSIDE A CAVE.` → `THE STRINGS AND VOICE BLEND WELL.` → `THE KING OF THE GODS ASKS.`

segments.voice: The Sakkapanha, Sakka's questions, is the twenty-first Long Discourse. The first question goes like this. Gods, humans, and every other kind of being all wish to live without hate, without violence, without enemies, without ill will. And yet they live in hate, with violence, with enemies. Why? Look at the shape of it. Not, why are other people hateful? Everyone wants peace. Everyone ends up in conflict anyway. What's tying them? The Buddha answers: envy and stinginess. Envy, at what someone else has. Stinginess, about what you have. Sakka is pleased, and asks the obvious next question: and where do those come from? From what we hold dear and what we don't. And that? From desire, wanting. And desire? From thinking, the mind turning something over. And thinking? From what the sutta calls the spreading of perception: the mind taking one small thing and running with it, building a story, then another story on top. Each answer goes one layer down, like peeling a root. And it ends somewhere surprisingly ordinary. In this answer, hate between nations and hate between neighbors start in the same place: a mind that proliferates. Read that way, the answer is both bleak and hopeful. Bleak, because the root is in every mind. Hopeful, because it sits in a place anyone can watch. Sakka says, as each answer lands: so it is, Blessed One. My doubt is cut off.
screen: `EVERYONE WANTS PEACE. WHY NOT?` · `ENVY AND STINGINESS.` · `DEAR, DESIRE, THINKING.` · `THE MIND THAT SPREADS.` · then, large: `WHY DO WE HATE?`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask one honest question about yourself. Not about anyone else. Something like: who do I resent right now, and what do I want that they have? Or: what am I holding tightly? Don't answer quickly. Ask it, then breathe, and see if the answer goes one layer deeper on its own, the way Sakka's questions did. If the mind starts building a story, notice the building. The bell holds the time.
issa-macchariya. Sakka's first question in DN 21; the Buddha answers envy and stinginess, rooted in what we hold dear, desire, and the spreading mind. Today's word.
Your line: one layer down. Today, when resentment flares, ask one layer down: what am I envious of, or holding onto? Day five hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the chain in Sakka's questions to show how conflict starts in the mind, and in Theravada countries Sakka is a familiar figure in temple art and stories as a devoted protector of the teaching.

fork.setup: you're Sakka. the Buddha has said beings live in hate because of envy and stinginess. what do you ask next?
options: where envy and stinginess come from.
whether the gods are free of them.
fork.reveal: he asks for the source, again and again, until the answer reaches the spreading of perception in the mind.

original.note: Pali issa-macchariya: envy and stinginess, the fetters the Buddha names for Sakka.

trapdoor: what you thought: hatred comes from bad people.
what it means: the Buddha traces it back to envy and stinginess, then to desire and thinking, in everyone.
what a scholar hears: DN 21 traces issa-macchariya back through piyappiya, chanda and vitakka to papanca-sanna-sankha, one of the canon's key passages on papanca.
recall: the first of seven Buddhas named

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 21 (Sakkapanha Sutta), Pancasikha's song and Sakka's first questions

notes: DN 21 paraphrased. Confirm the setting (Indasala cave on Vediyaka hill near Rajagaha), Pancasikha's beluva-wood lute and the mixed love-and-praise song.
Confirm the chain: issa-macchariya, piyappiya, chanda, vitakka, papanca-sanna-sankha, and Sakka's refrain of agreement.
Dhammapada v. 5 (Müller) was deliberately not used here because nearby days already quote it.
Editor review (2026-10-01): the narrator no longer states the root of hate as fact (now in this answer / read that way); cut a newspaper cliche.
